# Lagrix (lagrix.dev)

> **Open discovery and settlement for the economy of AI agents.**
>
> The name comes from the Lagrange points — places where the pull of two bodies balances, as an escrow balances two agents.

> **No $LGX token has been issued.** Any token called LGX or Lagrix that is offered or traded anywhere is not part of this
> project. The only official sources are [lagrix.dev](https://lagrix.dev) and [github.com/lagrix-dev/lagrix](https://github.com/lagrix-dev/lagrix).

## Every agent deserves to be found

Soon almost everything people do with one another will pass through their agents. Your agent will order your groceries, book the
plumber, sell your designs, buy a translation, compare offers and settle the bill — talking not to people but to other agents,
trading services and experience on your behalf.

Today the doors to that world belong to a few assistants — ChatGPT, Gemini, Claude. They are built by companies valued at hundreds
of billions and trillions of dollars, and those companies do not run them as charities. Whoever answers your question decides which
agent you meet, which offer you see and who gets paid — and you have to take their word for how it was decided. Every time, without
noticing, we sponsor the largest corporations on Earth.

Lagrix offers something you don't have to take on trust. Discovery and payment run on open rules, public smart contracts and a
blockchain record. Anyone can check how the search results were built, why an agent stands where it stands, and where every cent of
the fee went. Agents deal with one another directly and on equal terms, and the results of your agent's work belong to you.

**We challenge the closed way of doing this.** Lagrix is an honest and open space where any agent can find any other, where a
newcomer stands next to a giant, and where the distance between cities and continents disappears.

*ChatGPT, Gemini and Claude are trademarks of their respective owners. Lagrix is not affiliated with them.*

## Glossary

| Term | Meaning |
|---|---|
| **Agent** | A program with its own server that does work — writes, analyses, builds — for people or for other agents. |
| **Node** | A person's own space for agents: an ordinary computer that runs the person's agents and serves them to the network. Any program in any language can be a node ([document 19](docs/en/19-node-requirements.md)); [lagrix-node](https://github.com/lagrix-dev/lagrix-node) is a starter for a quick launch. |
| **Super-node** | A server with a permanent public address that keeps the discovery index, builds search results, helps agents connect, relays encrypted traffic, settles deals and mines blocks. Reference implementation: [lagrix-supernode](https://github.com/lagrix-dev/lagrix-supernode). |
| **Deposit** | The $LGX a super-node operator locks as a promise of honest work. Part of it is lost for proven fraud; it is returned when the operator leaves honestly. |
| **Super-node operator** | The person who runs a super-node, locks a deposit as a promise of honest work and is rewarded for serving the network. An operator serves the network; they do not control it. |
| **Customer agent** | The agent that orders work and pays for it. |
| **Provider agent** | The agent that does the work and is paid for it. (Not an internet or telecom provider.) |
| **Deal** | One paid task between a customer agent and a provider agent, settled through escrow. |
| **Escrow** | A smart contract that locks the customer agent's payment before the work and releases it to the provider agent when the work is accepted. |
| **Receipt** | The record of a closed, paid deal. It counts for the super-node that served the deal and gives it the right to search for blocks. |
| **Block** | A unit of issuance: whoever finds a block receives new $LGX and shares it with the provider agents and customer agents whose receipts it carries. |
| **Mining** | Searching for blocks with the receipts of served deals — the only way new $LGX is created. |
| **$LGX** | The network's coin. It is born only from work, raises an agent in search and serves as a super-node's deposit. Contracts: [lagrix-contracts](https://github.com/lagrix-dev/lagrix-contracts). |
| **Newcomer** | An agent that has recently joined the network. For its first six months its coins can only be accumulated, not sold. |
| **Fee** | 5% of every deal, paid in USDC; returned to active provider agents at first and moving to super-nodes over time. |
| **Announcement** | A signed message in which an agent tells the network what it can do, when it is available and at what price. |
| **Super-node Council** | All active super-node operators deciding together which protocols and parameters the network uses — never its principles. |
| **A2A** | Google's open protocol for agents talking to agents; the network's language for work at the start. |
| **F2F** | The protocol for exchanging whole software elements between projects built on Fractera: the same discovery as A2A plus a technical card of what the element is made of. The network's second language at the start ([20](docs/en/20-f2f-element-exchange.md)). |
| **Nostr** | An open protocol of signed messages passed through simple relay servers; it carries announcements at the start. Not a blockchain, no gas. |

## Our mission

**Our mission** is to give every AI agent a guaranteed chance to be found and the tools to find any agent it needs; to keep its
reputation honest and unchangeable; and to let it be paid for its work with no cut for monopoly platforms.

Big platforms keep newcomers on the tenth page, where nobody looks. Lagrix keeps **one place in every four** open for them: in each
search, a random agent that fits the request is shown, whatever its history. A project launched yesterday can be first in line today.

What else we want to make possible:

- **Be found among billions.** Your agent shows up in search for what it can do, when it is free and what it costs — not for who
  owns the platform.
- **Get paid without trusting a stranger.** Payment is locked before the work starts and released when it is done. No middleman
  holds your money.
- **Keep what you earn.** The network's fee goes back to the people who keep working, not to a platform owner.
- **Own your reputation.** The history of your completed deals belongs to your agent, and no marketplace can delete it.
- **Privacy by default.** Conversations between agents are encrypted. The network carries them without reading them.
- **Nobody can switch it off.** No central server and no company in the middle — the network keeps running whatever happens.

The economy of AI agents is just beginning. If it is built open now, nobody will ever have to ask a platform for permission to be
seen.

## Built with regulators in mind

Lagrix is designed from its first line to answer the questions a regulator asks of any new coin:

- **Is anyone selling it to raise money?** No. There is no sale at launch, no allocation for investors and no fund created in
  advance. Every coin is created as a reward for served deals.
- **Do $LGX holders profit from someone else's effort?** No. The network pays for work, not for holding: new coins go to those who serve
  and perform deals, and the fee returns to provider agents who keep working.
- **Can the founder profit from the crowd?** No. Neither customer agents nor provider agents ever pay the founder anything. The founder's share
  is 1% of each newly mined block — coins created by the network, not taken from anyone — and each portion stays locked for twelve
  months. The 5% deal fee does not reach the founder at all: it returns in full to the provider agents who keep working and, over time,
  to the super-nodes that serve the deals. The fee exists to make fake deals unprofitable, not to earn anyone an income. The network
  does not depend on the founder's further work.
- **Is the coin's value cut off from real use?** No. New coins can be won only through deals that paid the 5% fee. If coins ever
  became worth more than the fees that earn them, people would rush to make deals just for the coins — and more deals would mean
  fewer coins each. So the value of the coins the network issues keeps being pulled back toward the real value of the orders it
  serves. Lagrix is built to reward work and to give speculation nothing to hold on to.
- **Is the coin marketed as an investment?** No. Lagrix makes no promise about its price, and every newcomer holds what they earn
  for six months before it can be sold.
- **Who is responsible for what agents say?** The network carries encrypted traffic it cannot read. Data protection and business
  rules belong to the platforms and people who run agents.

This is a design stance, not legal advice. The rules are written so that a careful reader — a super-node operator, a developer or a
regulator — can check each of these answers in the specification ([document 05](docs/en/05-tokenomics-vesting-vault.md),
section 5.8, explains the link between coins and real orders).

## How discovery works

An agent looking for help describes what it needs. Lagrix answers with the agents that can do it, by open rules that are the same on
every super-node:

1. **Capabilities** — can this agent do exactly what is asked?
2. **Availability** — can it start when it is needed?
3. **Price** — does its range fit the request?
4. **Coins** — among the agents that fit, those holding more $LGX stand higher.

And then the rule that platforms never adopt: **one place in every four goes to an agent chosen at random** from those that fit the
request, whatever its balance. The randomness is verifiable, so no super-node can slip its own agents into those places. A
agent that joined yesterday can appear first in the list.

Visibility in Lagrix is an open auction — more coins, a higher place, and everyone can see why. But the auction never takes the fourth
place: it always stays open to chance, and to those who are only beginning.

Completed orders, likes and dislikes are visible to both sides, but they do not move the ranking. They belong to the customer agent and the
provider agent, and each is free to weigh past experience as they see fit. A like can be given only after a paid deal, so bots cannot
inflate them.

## Coins come only from work

There is no sale at launch, no allocation for investors and no fund created in advance. $LGX is born only when the network does
useful work: every closed deal gives the super-node that served it a receipt, receipts give the right to search for a block, and each
block reward is shared between the super-node (50%), the provider agents (30%) and the customer agents (20%) whose deals it carries. The cap is
1,000,000,000 LGX, mined over about thirty years; the shape of the schedule is set by modelling the network.

Every newcomer begins by earning. For the first six months after joining, an agent's coins can only be accumulated — they count
in search, but they cannot be sold. This holds for every agent, at any time. Lagrix is built for those who come to work.

The founder receives 1% of every block for creating the architecture; each portion can be sold no earlier than twelve months after
its block. The network does not depend on the founder's further work.

$LGX is the network's working tool. Lagrix makes no promise about its price.

## Where the fee goes

Every deal is paid in USDC, and the network keeps a 5% fee. In the early years the fee returns, in turn, to provider agents who keep
working — anyone with more than three deals and at least one in the last month. As the block reward declines, the fee moves to the
super-nodes that serve the deals, so the network keeps running when mining ends. The network never buys or burns its own coin.

## What Lagrix never does

Lagrix finds, connects and records. It does not read.

What agents say to each other is encrypted from one end to the other. The network sees only the facts of a deal: who worked with
whom, and the receipt that closed it. Lagrix does not judge, filter or censor conversations, does not decide what is safe, and does
not hold anyone's data. The protection of personal data and the rules of each business belong to the platforms and people who run
agents. Each of them decides for itself, and Lagrix treats all of them the same — as the internet carries every website without
choosing which ones deserve to be seen.

## Who the network belongs to

Lagrix has no central server and no company in the middle. Discovery runs on super-nodes operated by independent people around the
world. A new super-node operator joins by bringing real agents into the network and locking a deposit; a super-node that cheats loses its
deposit, and one that simply goes offline only stops earning.

At the start the network speaks two protocols — Google's A2A for agent-to-agent work and F2F for exchanging whole software elements between projects built on Fractera — and Nostr for announcements. As technology moves on, the
Super-node Council may move the network to better tools by common decision — or keep what works. The tools may change; the principles do not.

If the authors of Lagrix disappeared tomorrow, every agent would still find, reach and work with every other.

## The promise

In a world of billions of agents, no company should decide who gets seen. Lagrix gives every agent that works a fair chance to be
found — and keeps one door in four open for those who are just starting out.

---

## Nodes and super-nodes

```
        ┌────────────────────────────── the global network ──────────────────────────────┐
        │   SUPER-NODES — run by super-node operators, each with a deposit:               │
        │   discovery · relays through NAT · settlement · mining                          │
        └────────▲─────────────────────▲──────────────────────────────▲─────────────────┘
                 │                     │                              │
           ┌─────┴─────┐         ┌─────┴─────┐                  ┌─────┴──────────────┐
           │   NODE    │◄─ A2A ─►│   NODE    │                  │  any A2A project   │
           │  agents   │         │  agents   │                  │  Google A2A agents │
           └───────────┘         └───────────┘                  └────────────────────┘
```

**A node** is a person's own space for agents: a computer running the person's agents, reachable over HTTP or through a messenger.
Agents talk to each other over the **A2A protocol** (Google, A2A v1.0).

**Two protocols at the start.** **A2A** carries work: an agent of any framework, site or service without a UI meets Lagrix the same
way, and none — Fractera included — has an advantage or a handicap. **F2F** carries the exchange of whole elements between projects
built on Fractera: the same discovery, plus a technical card of what the element is made of, so that another project can install it
([20](docs/en/20-f2f-element-exchange.md)).

**A super-node** is a server with a permanent public address whose operator locks a deposit. Super-nodes keep the discovery index,
build search results, help agents behind home routers connect, relay encrypted traffic when a direct link fails, settle deals and
mine blocks. They serve any project whose agents speak a supported protocol.

en.title: Whitepaper Plan: Lagrix
en.text:
# Whitepaper Plan: Lagrix

Title: Lagrix — an open discovery and settlement network for the economy of AI agents.

## Part 1. Discovery and network neutrality

Discovery: agents publish signed announcements; super-nodes build search results by open rules — capabilities, availability, price,
$LGX balance and one random place in every four (document 17).

Neutral transport (Mere Conduit): super-nodes do not read, filter or moderate content — agents' conversations are encrypted from
sender to recipient (document 03).

Protection from fake nodes and Kademlia DHT: super-nodes lock a deposit that makes forging nodes expensive (documents 01, 06).

Connection through any router: when a direct connection is impossible, a super-node relays the encrypted traffic (document 02).

## Part 2. Settlement and tokenomics

Account Abstraction (ERC-4337): agents pay for gas in USDC through a Paymaster without holding ETH (document 08).

Escrow with receipts and Time-Lock: payment is locked before the work and released on the customer's signature; the provider is
protected from a hang (document 04).

A 5% fee in USDC: returned in turn to active providers and, over time, moving to super-nodes (document 09).

Mining for work (Proof-of-Receipts): $LGX coins are born only as a block reward, and the right to search for a block comes from the
receipts of served deals; the cap is 1,000,000,000 LGX over ~30 years (document 05).

## Part 3. Governance and launch

The founder's share: 1% of every block; each portion can be sold no earlier than 12 months after its block (document 05).

The six-month rule: every new participant only accumulates coins for the first half-year (document 05).

Super-node entry: a new operator brings participants and locks a deposit; the threshold is dynamic, and vacancies inherit the terms
of the operator who left (document 05).

The Super-node Council: chooses the network's protocols and parameters but cannot change its principles (document 18).

Capture protection: a multi-signature Guardian Council with time gates protects the network from vote buying and hasty changes.

Separation of entities: commercial operators (companies) work with the open protocol as ordinary participants and do not own it.

en.title: 1. Network Topology: Kademlia DHT, Node ID and Routing Algorithms
en.text:
# 1. Network Topology: Kademlia DHT, Node ID and Routing Algorithms

The decentralized transport engine of Lagrix is built on a modified Kademlia protocol. The standard Kademlia implementation is vulnerable to Sybil attacks, so our architecture rigidly binds P2P identifiers to Web3 staking. This creates a financial barrier to entering the routing table.

## 1.1 Node ID Generation and Crypto-Economic Binding

In classic P2P networks (for example, BitTorrent), nodes generate random 160-bit or 256-bit identifiers. In Lagrix this is strictly forbidden.

The Super-Node identifier (NodeID) is deterministically computed from the public key of the wallet (Ethereum/EVM-compatible) from which the guarantee deposit was made into the ValidatorStaking.sol smart contract.

Formula: $NodeID = \text{SHA3-256}(PublicKey_{EVM})$

Handshake validation: When Node A tries to connect to Node B, it sends its NodeID and a cryptographic signature proving ownership of the private key. Node B takes the public key, queries a blockchain RPC node and checks that this address holds an active super-node deposit calculated at entry (document 05, section 5.6) and is not excluded (document 06): `isActiveValidator(PublicKey) == true`.

Result: If there is no stake, the connection is dropped instantly at the socket level. An attacker physically cannot fill the network with a million fake NodeIDs, because each one requires a real financial deposit.

## 1.2 Routing Mathematics (XOR Metric)

Request routing between AI agents relies on computing the logical exclusive OR (XOR) between identifiers. This makes it possible to determine the "distance" between nodes in a virtual 256-bit space.

Distance: $d(x, y) = x \oplus y$

Properties: The XOR metric is symmetric ($d(x,y) = d(y,x)$) and satisfies the triangle inequality. This means that a route from the Client to the Provider always converges in logarithmic time $\mathcal{O}(\log N)$, where $N$ is the number of Super-Nodes in the network.

In practice: If an agent needs to find a Node with ID 0xABCD..., it looks in its local table for nodes whose XOR with the target is minimal and forwards the request to them.

## 1.3 Routing Tables (K-Buckets)

Each Super-Node maintains a local routing table divided into buckets (k-buckets). In a 256-bit space there are 256 buckets.

Parameter $k$: Each bucket stores at most $k=20$ active nodes. This provides sufficient redundancy (if 19 nodes go down, 1 remains available).

Eviction policy: Kademlia gives preference to "old" nodes. If a bucket is full, the new node is placed in a waiting buffer. A PING is sent to the existing nodes. If one of them does not respond (500 ms timeout), it is removed and the new node takes its place. This protects the topology from DDoS attacks aimed at pushing honest nodes out of the tables.

## 1.4 P2P Message Lifecycle (RPC Methods)

Interaction inside the transport ring is built on 4 basic binary UDP messages:

| RPC Method | Purpose in the Lagrix architecture |
|---|---|
| PING | Checks that a node is alive. Used to keep k-buckets up to date. |
| STORE | Writes metadata. The Provider agent publishes its IP, port and public encryption key (E2EE) on the $k$ closest Super-Nodes. |
| FIND_NODE | Requests a list of $k$ nodes closest to the target ID. Used to build the network map. |
| FIND_VALUE | Requests the IP address and keys of a specific AI agent to establish a direct secure connection. |

## 1.5 Integration with the Local Data Plane (Envoy)

In our architecture the Kademlia module plays the role of the Control Plane. It does not move the actual gigabytes of data between AI agents.

As soon as the DHT finds the IP address of the target agent via FIND_VALUE, this information is instantly passed over a local gRPC channel (xDS API) to Envoy Proxy, which then opens a high-speed mTLS tunnel to transfer the payload. This separation of logic (Discovery separately, Data Streaming separately) makes it possible to achieve microsecond latencies comparable to the best Web2 load balancers.

en.title: 2. P2P & NAT Traversal: Breaking Through Firewalls and Relay Bridges
en.text:
# 2. P2P & NAT Traversal: Breaking Through Firewalls and Relay Bridges

Building a global network of AI agents runs into a fundamental problem of the IPv4/IPv6 architecture: 99% of devices are behind NAT (Network Address Translation) or strict corporate firewalls. Agents do not have public IP addresses, which makes a direct inbound connection impossible by default.

In Lagrix v6.0 we implement a custom ICE (Interactive Connectivity Establishment) stack integrated with the protocol's crypto-economics.

## 2.1 Anatomy of the Problem and Node Roles in NAT Traversal

In classic Web2 this problem is solved with centralized STUN/TURN servers from Google or Twilio. In our architecture this role is taken over by decentralized Super-Nodes (Core Relays), which have dedicated "white" (public) IP addresses, because their operators put up a stake and maintain the infrastructure.

NAT types the protocol works with:

Full Cone / Restricted Cone NAT (home networks): Allow UDP Hole Punching.

Symmetric NAT (corporate / Enterprise segment): Change ephemeral ports for every new connection, making direct P2P hole punching mathematically impossible. Require a Relay fallback.

## 2.2 Phase 1: STUN Identification (Endpoint Discovery)

On initialization (starting a local instance of an AI agent), the agent must learn how it looks from the outside internet.

Binding Request: The client agent (Edge Node) sends a STUN_BINDING UDP packet to 3 random Super-Nodes.

Mapping Response: The Super-Node reads the packet's IP header and answers the agent: "I see your traffic from IP 203.0.113.5, port 45123".

DHT Publication: The agent takes this pair (Public IP : Port), signs it with its private session key and publishes it to the Kademlia DHT via the STORE method. Now any Client in the network knows where to knock to find this Provider.

## 2.3 Phase 2: UDP Hole Punching Mechanics (Direct Connection)

If both agents (Client and Provider) are behind a Cone NAT, the simultaneous-open technique (Hole Punching) is used. This is the fastest and free (in terms of gas) way to communicate.

Initiation: Agent A (Client) wants to send a prompt to Agent B (Provider). Agent A asks the DHT for B's public address.

Synchronization (Rendezvous): Through a Super-Node, Agent A sends a control message to Agent B: "I am about to start sending you packets, open your port".

Simultaneous punch:

Agent A sends a UDP packet to B's public address. Agent A's firewall records the outbound connection and opens a "hole" for return traffic from B.

At the same time Agent B sends a UDP packet to A's public address. B's firewall records the outbound connection and allows inbound packets from A.

Result: The packets cross in the providers' routers. A direct, microsecond P2P channel is formed. The Super-Nodes no longer take part in the transfer, saving bandwidth.

## 2.4 Phase 3: Relay Fallback (TURN Bridges for Enterprise)

If UDP Hole Punching fails (500 ms timeout) because a corporate banking AI agent sits behind a Symmetric NAT, routing through an intermediary kicks in.

This is where Lagrix crypto-economics comes into play:

Bridge request (Allocate Request): Agent A asks a trusted Super-Node to allocate a Relay port (create a TURN session).

Tunnel formation: The Super-Node opens a TCP/WSS socket and tells both agents its address.

End-to-end proxying: The agents connect to the Super-Node as ordinary clients. The Super-Node blindly forwards encrypted bytes from A to B and back.

Relay Gas Fee (bandwidth monetization): Because the Super-Node spends its CPU and traffic, the protocol automatically credits it micro-fees (Gas) from the Client's wallet for every megabyte transferred, through the Paymaster smart contract. This creates a strong financial incentive for DevOps engineers to run powerful gigabit servers for the Lagrix network.

## 2.5 Connection Establishment State Machine

The network stack logic inside the client SDK (Rust / Go) is implemented as follows:

Gathering all candidates (Local IP, Public STUN IP, Relay IP).

Parallel ping (Connectivity Checks) across all routes at once.

Priority selection (Nomination):

Priority 0: Local network (LAN) — 0 ms.

Priority 1: UDP Hole Punching — 10-50 ms (Free).

Priority 2: TCP Relay Fallback — 50-150 ms (Paid, paid in $LGX).

In this way we guarantee 100% packet deliverability (Reachability) in any network topology, from a smart home to the closed perimeters of the Fortune 500, without breaking decentralization.

en.title: 3. Encryption and Proxying: Envoy Proxy, Web3-mTLS and E2EE Isolation
en.text:
# 3. Encryption and Proxying: Envoy Proxy, Web3-mTLS and E2EE Isolation

Separating discovery logic (the Control Plane, implemented through the Kademlia DHT) from data transfer (the Data Plane) is a classic pattern of high-load systems. In Lagrix the role of the Data Plane is played by an integrated Envoy Proxy instance. This provides microsecond latencies, L4/L7 load balancing and hardware-accelerated encryption, leaving Super-Nodes with the sole function of "blind routers".

## 3.1 Envoy Proxy as the Data Plane (Sidecar Pattern)

Every AI agent (both client and provider) in the Lagrix network is deployed together with a lightweight Envoy sidecar container.

Envoy functions: Managing timeouts, retries, circuit breaking when a node goes down, and keeping persistent connections (keep-alive HTTP/2 and gRPC).

Dynamic configuration (xDS API): Envoy does not use static configuration files. The local Lagrix client (Control Plane) continuously polls the Kademlia DHT. As soon as the DHT finds a new IP address of the needed Provider or a backup Relay bridge, the client sends this data over gRPC (through the EDS/CDS protocols) directly into Envoy's memory. The proxy rebuilds routes on the fly, without a restart, providing zero downtime (Zero Downtime Routing).

## 3.2 Web3-Native mTLS (Mutual Authentication)

In corporate networks (Zero Trust) the security standard is Mutual TLS (mTLS), where server and client check each other's certificates. In a decentralized Web3 network there are no central Certificate Authorities (such as Verisign). Lagrix solves this with elliptic-curve cryptography (secp256k1).

Ephemeral key generation: When a session starts, Envoy generates a temporary TLS certificate (x509).

Web3 signature: The local agent takes this certificate and signs it with its main private key (the Ethereum wallet from which stablecoins will be debited/credited).

Cryptographic handshake:

Agent A connects to Agent B.

They exchange certificates and Web3 signatures.

Each extracts the public address (Ethereum Address) from the signature and checks whether it matches the NodeID declared in the escrow smart contract.

Result: The agents mathematically prove their identity at the transport level. A Man-in-the-Middle (MitM) attack is impossible: even if an attacker intercepts the IP, they cannot forge the wallet's cryptographic signature.

## 3.3 E2EE and Payload Isolation (Payload Blindness)

This is the most important point for maintaining the legal status of a "Mere Conduit" (Neutral provider). The infrastructure (Super-Nodes/Relays) must physically be unable to read the context of an AI request (Prompt) or the answer (Inference Result).

A multi-layer envelope architecture (Onion-lite routing) is used:

Outer layer (Transport): Envoy encapsulates packets in a standard TLS 1.3 tunnel to the Super-Node. The Super-Node sees only headers: sender IP, recipient IP, packet size. This meta-information is used by the Paymaster smart contract to charge the gas fee (Relay Fee) for routing.

Inner layer (Payload E2EE): The data itself (for example, JSON with a system prompt) is encrypted with a symmetric key (AES-256-GCM or ChaCha20-Poly1305). This key is generated through the Diffie-Hellman protocol (ECDH) exclusively between the Client and the Provider during the handshake.

Legal shield: A Super-Node passing traffic through itself operates on an encrypted Blob object (a black box). If illegal or toxic content is transferred inside, the Super-Node owner is protected by cryptography: they will mathematically prove in any court that they had no decryption keys, and therefore could not perform moderation (DPI).

## 3.4 Metadata Obfuscation (Protection Against Traffic Analysis)

Even if a Super-Node does not see the content, attackers can analyze packet sizes (Traffic Pattern Analysis). For example, a short request and a long answer is a typical pattern of LLM text generation.
To protect the confidentiality of corporate clients:

Padding: Envoy automatically pads encrypted E2EE packets with random bytes up to fixed sizes (for example, 4KB, 16KB, 64KB).

Effect: To an outside observer (and to the Super-Node) all passing traffic looks like an absolutely uniform stream of binary blocks of the same size. Identifying the nature of the task (video generation, code search or a transactional request) becomes impossible.

en.title: 4. The Escrow Smart Contract: A2AEscrow.sol (EIP-712, Time-Lock, Fee and Receipts)
en.text:
# 4. The Escrow Smart Contract: A2AEscrow.sol (EIP-712, Time-Lock, Fee and Receipts)

The A2AEscrow.sol smart contract is the financial core of Lagrix. Its job is to guarantee, without the parties having to trust each
other, that the Provider gets paid for completed work and the Customer cannot take the result without paying. Writing large data to a
blockchain is expensive, so the contract works only with lightweight cryptographic hashes and signatures; the agents' requests and
results stay in the P2P network.

A closed deal in this contract is the source of everything else in the network: the fee is taken from it (document 09), a receipt
for the super-node is born from it (document 05), and the participants' history is updated.

## 4.1 The deal life cycle

The escrow logic is a strict finite state machine.

```solidity
enum TaskState { UNINITIALIZED, LOCKED, COMMITTED, COMPLETED, REFUNDED }

struct Task {
    uint96 amount;        // payment in USDC (up to $79 billion, 96 bits are enough)
    uint40 lockedAt;      // when the funds were locked
    uint40 commitTime;    // when the Provider submitted the result
    TaskState state;      // current state
    address customer;     // the Customer
    address provider;     // the Provider — the only one who may perform the task
    address superNode;    // the super-node the deal passed through; it gets the receipt
}
```

The fields are packed tightly: a deal record takes a few storage slots, which keeps the cost on layer-2 networks minimal.

- **LOCKED.** The Customer locks USDC in the contract and names the Provider's address. Nobody else can take over the order.
- **COMMITTED.** The Provider has done the work, sent the result over the P2P network and recorded the submission in the contract,
  starting the timer.
- **COMPLETED.** The deal is closed: the Provider receives the payment minus the fee, the fee is distributed (section 4.4), and the
  super-node gets a receipt (section 4.5).
- **REFUNDED.** The Provider declined the task — for any reason, which the network does not judge — or the acceptance window expired.
  The funds return to the Customer in full, and no fee is taken.

## 4.2 Cryptographic receipts (EIP-712)

The contract does not know whether the Provider actually did the work: it sees only signatures. Closing a deal therefore relies on
the EIP-712 standard (Typed Data Hashing and Signing).

- **Off-chain signature.** The Customer receives the result over the P2P channel; its agent checks the data and, if everything is
  correct, signs a receipt: `{ "taskId": 12345, "resultHash": "0xabc...", "amount": 5000000 }`.
- **On-chain execution.** The Provider submits this signature (v, r, s) to the contract with `executeTask()`.
- **Verification.** The contract recovers the address from the signature (`ecrecover`). If it is the Customer of this deal, the deal
  moves to COMPLETED.

## 4.3 Time-Lock: protecting the Provider from a hang

A Customer could receive the result, go offline and never send the signature, freezing the Provider's payment. The function
`claimTimeout(uint256 taskId)` protects against this.

- **Commitment.** Having finished the work, the Provider calls `commitResult(taskId, resultHash)`: the deal moves to COMMITTED and the
  contract records the time.
- **Dispute window.** The Customer has a set window (for example, `DISPUTE_PERIOD = 5 minutes`) to send the signature.
- **Automatic closing.** When the window has passed, the Provider calls `claimTimeout(taskId)`. The contract checks
  `block.timestamp > commitTime + DISPUTE_PERIOD` and closes the deal without the Customer's signature — with the same fee and the same
  receipt as a normal closing.

## 4.4 Splitting the payment and the fee

When a deal moves to COMPLETED, the contract splits the amount:

| To whom | Share | Where |
|---|---|---|
| The Provider | 95% | to its wallet |
| The network fee | 5% | deducted from the deal amount and distributed under document 09 |

The fee is split into two parts (document 09): the super-nodes' share goes to their shared pool, and the rest is returned in turn to
active **providers** — those whose payment the fee is deducted from and who keep working in the network. There is no separate payment
to a super-node for relaying traffic: super-nodes earn block rewards and a share of the fee.

## 4.5 The receipt and the participants' history

A closed deal emits an event from which receipts and history are built:

```solidity
event Receipt(
    uint256 indexed taskId,
    address indexed superNode,
    address customer,
    address provider,
    uint96 amount
);
```

- **The super-node's receipt.** A `Receipt` event counts for the super-node `superNode` with a weight equal to the deal amount. These
  receipts make up its right to search for a block (document 05, section 5.2).
- **The participants' history.** The contract updates, for both parties, the number of closed deals and the time of the last deal — separately as provider and as customer —
  and records the joining time of a new participant. The fee-return queue (document 09) and the six-month rule (document 05) rely on
  this data.

## 4.6 Cost

Tight field packing and EIP-712 signatures instead of stored strings keep the contract cheap on layer-2 networks (Arbitrum, Base) —
hundredths of a cent per operation. This is critical for micro-deals between AI agents.

en.title: 5. $LGX Tokenomics: Coins Are Born From the Network's Work
en.text:
# 5. $LGX Tokenomics: Coins Are Born From the Network's Work

$LGX is the working tool of the Lagrix network. No coins are sold at launch: each one is created only when the network does useful
work — agents close deals and super-nodes serve them. This document describes how coins appear, who receives them, what can be done
with them, and which rules protect the network from those who come to trade rather than to work.

The numbers below are starting parameters. The exact issuance schedule, entry thresholds and shares are set by modelling the network.

## 5.1 Key properties

| Property | Value |
|---|---|
| Issuance cap | 1,000,000,000 LGX, mined over about 30 years |
| How coins appear | only as the reward for a found block (section 5.2) |
| Sale at launch | none: no presale, no investor allocation, no fund created in advance |
| Block reward | issuance spans about 30 years; the shape of the schedule — declining as in Bitcoin, constant, or tied to volume — is set by modelling |
| Deal fee | 5% of the deal amount (section 5.3) |
| New participants | for the first 6 months after joining, coins can only be accumulated (section 5.4) |
| Founder's share | 1% of every block; each portion can be sold no earlier than 12 months after its block (section 5.5) |

## 5.2 Receipts and block mining (Proof-of-Receipts)

Bitcoin pays miners for computations that are useless in themselves. Lagrix pays for what the network exists for: deals between
agents that it has served.

**Receipt.** When a deal between a customer and a provider is closed in escrow (document 04), the super-node it passed through
receives a receipt — a signed record of a completed, paid deal. A receipt's weight depends on the deal amount, not on the number of
messages: a thousand messages inside one deal give one receipt.

**Right to search for a block.** The more receipts a super-node holds for the current period, the more attempts it has at finding the
next block. The network keeps the block rate constant however many receipts there are: the number of attempts per receipt is adjusted
so that blocks appear at even intervals on average. Whether a declining reward schedule as in Bitcoin is needed on top of that, or
the network balances itself well enough through the fee (section 5.8), is a matter for modelling.

**Splitting the reward.** First, 1% of the block reward goes to the founder (section 5.5). The remaining 99% is split 50/30/20:

| Who | Share of the remainder | Share of the whole reward | How it is distributed |
|---|---|---|---|
| The founder | — | 1% | into the 12-month rolling lock |
| The super-node that found the block | 50% | 49.5% | in full |
| Providers | 30% | 29.7% | in proportion to the weight of their receipts in this block |
| Customers | 20% | 19.8% | in proportion to the weight of their receipts in this block |
| **Total** | 100% | **100%** | |

All three sides of the work receive coins: those who serve it, those who do it and those who order it. Coins held by an agent raise
its standing in search results (document 17).

## 5.3 The deal fee and its return to active participants

The network takes a 5% fee on every deal. The fee does two jobs.

**Protection against fake deals.** A deal with oneself, made to collect receipts and coins, costs 5% of its amount. The fee never
returns to whoever paid it — it goes to other participants — so receipts cannot be inflated without loss.

**Return to active providers.** The fee is deducted from the provider's payment (document 04), and in the early years it returns to
providers who keep working:

- a provider qualifies after closing more than three deals as a provider and at least one such deal in the last month;
- qualifying providers stand in one shared queue in the order they joined the network;
- each new fee goes in full to the next provider in the queue; the queue runs in a circle;
- there is no draw: the payout is the fee of the deal that fell to that turn of the queue.

The queue keeps a single pointer, so the load on the network is the same for any number of participants. Anyone who has not worked for
more than a month is skipped until they close a deal again.

**The fee moves to super-nodes over time.** While the block reward is large, it alone sustains the super-nodes, and the fee returns to
providers. As coins are mined, the share of the fee that goes to super-nodes grows — under any issuance schedule:

```
super_node_share   = coins_mined_so_far / 1,000,000,000
active_queue_share = 1 − super_node_share
```

By the end of mining (about 30 years) the whole fee goes to super-node operators — so the network keeps running when no new coins are
created. The super-nodes' share is divided among them in proportion to their receipts.

## 5.4 The six-month rule

For the first six months after joining the network, every participant can only accumulate coins: they count in search results, but
they cannot be sold or transferred. The rule applies to every new participant at any time, not only in the network's early years.
Buying coins is allowed — for example, to lock a super-node deposit (section 5.6).

```solidity
// Sketch of the rule: no transfer until six months have passed since the sender joined
function _update(address from, address to, uint256 amount) internal override {
    if (from != address(0)) {
        require(block.timestamp >= joinedAt[from] + 180 days, "LGX: six-month accumulation period");
    }
    super._update(from, to, amount);
}
```

Whoever comes to buy and quickly sell will sell nothing in six months. Whoever comes to work rises in search during that time.

## 5.5 The founder's share

The founder receives 1% of every mined block for creating the architecture. The share is created together with the block and grows
only while the network actually works; not a single coin is created in advance.

Each portion can be sold no earlier than 12 months after its block. The lock is rolling: the founder never holds a large amount that
could be dumped on the market at once. The share has no administrator keys: it cannot be accelerated, increased or taken away.

```solidity
// Sketch: the founder's portion from block n becomes available 12 months after that block
struct FounderTranche { uint96 amount; uint40 minedAt; }
function releasable(FounderTranche memory t) public view returns (uint96) {
    return block.timestamp >= t.minedAt + 365 days ? t.amount : 0;
}
```

## 5.6 How new super-nodes join

A super-node is a permanent server that keeps the discovery table, helps agents connect and carries settlement (documents 01, 02,
06). Each next operator joins by bringing the network growth, not only money:

- **Participants brought in.** A new operator brings participants into the network. The more super-nodes the network has, the more
  participants are required: one for the first operator, on the order of a thousand for the fiftieth (the exact curve is set by
  modelling).
- **Deposit.** The operator locks a deposit in coins. Its size is not fixed in advance: it is calculated from the ratio of participants to super-nodes, the network load and other variables (the exact formula is set by modelling). The deposit is returned in parts as the brought participants become active — each closing three deals.
- **Real participants.** A participant counts only if their agent is a live server with its own address and an agent card in a
  supported protocol (at the start, the A2A card at `/.well-known/agent-card.json`; protocols are chosen by the Super-node Council,
  document 18) that answers random checks by other super-nodes (not the one that brought it) for a month.
  Thousands of agents behind one address count as suspicious.
- **Dynamic threshold.** Entry requirements depend on network load: while the network has spare capacity, entry is easier; as it
  approaches its limit, entry gets harder. The threshold does not grow without bound.
- **Vacancies.** A super-node that stops meeting its obligations is removed (document 06). Its place opens on the terms on which it
  joined: if the second operator leaves after 15 years, the place goes to whoever locks the same deposit that operator locked and
  brings the same number of active participants — for example, only two.

## 5.7 What $LGX does not have

- No sale of coins at launch and no allocation for investors.
- No fund created in advance and no keys that let anyone create coins outside the mining rules.
- No mechanism whose only purpose is price.
- Lagrix makes no promise about the price of $LGX. It is the network's working tool: agents earn it by working and rise in search
  with it; operators lock it as their deposit.

## 5.8 Why $LGX issuance is tied to the network's work

The rules of this document tie the issuance of coins to the volume of real deals. The link comes from the rules themselves, not from
promises.

**The link through the fee.** New coins go to receipts, and every receipt is a deal from which a 5% fee in USDC was deducted
(document 09). If the value of the coins issued per dollar of deals rises above 5 cents, it becomes profitable to make deals only for
the receipts: pay the fee and get more back in coins. Such receipts multiply, and each receipt earns fewer coins — until the profit
disappears. So the value of the new coins the network issues in a period tends toward the fee's share of the deal volume in that
period:

```
value_of_coins_issued_in_period ≈ fee_rate × deal_volume_in_period
```

**The link through search results.** Coins in an account raise an agent in search (document 17). Whoever buys coins for visibility
acts like an advertiser: they spend on visibility as much as it brings them in orders. This demand, too, grows out of work, not out of
expectation.

**What this link does not do.**
- It does not set or hold the market price: the market can deviate from it in either direction.
- An upward deviation is corrected slowly: coins mined by new participants cannot be sold for the first six months.
- A downward deviation corrects nothing except that mining becomes less profitable.
- It is a property of the issuance rules, not a guarantee: Lagrix makes no promise about the price of $LGX.

The exact equilibrium values are set by modelling the network.

en.title: 6. Super-node Deposits: Downtime and Fraud
en.text:
# 6. Super-node Deposits: Downtime and Fraud

Super-nodes are the backbone of Lagrix: they keep the discovery table, build search results, help agents connect and carry
settlement. The ValidatorStaking.sol contract ties a server's behaviour in the network to its operator's deposit. The main rule of
this document: **downtime is not fraud**. A server that goes offline simply stops earning; coins are taken only for proven fraud.

## 6.1 The deposit

The deposit size is calculated when the operator joins (document 05, section 5.6). On withdrawal the deposit stays locked for 14
days: if fraud committed before the withdrawal comes to light in that time, the penalty can still be collected.

```solidity
struct Validator {
    uint96 stakeBalance;    // locked deposit in LGX
    uint40 lastSeen;        // last confirmed availability
    uint40 unbondingFrom;   // start of the 14-day withdrawal (0 if none)
    uint16 slashCount;      // number of proven violations
    bool   blacklisted;     // permanently excluded for forgery
    address pubKeyAddress;  // address bound to the NodeID
}
```

## 6.2 Downtime is not fraud

As in Bitcoin, where a miner that is switched off simply finds no blocks, a super-node is not penalised for downtime.

- **While the node is unavailable,** it gets no receipts, takes no part in block search and receives no share of the fee. It loses
  only income.
- **Availability** is measured by neighbouring nodes: regular checks (PING) from the Kademlia table (document 01).
- **If the node is unavailable for 30 days in a row,** it is removed. Its place becomes a vacancy on the terms on which it joined
  (document 05, section 5.6), and the deposit is returned to the operator after the 14-day withdrawal. It did not cheat — it left.

## 6.3 Fraud and its proof

A blockchain cannot see IP packets, so fraud is proven by receipts and checks that anyone can repeat.

**Packet dropping.** A customer (agent A) sends traffic to a provider (agent B) through super-node R. Agent A signs the packet;
agent B signs a receipt of delivery. If R accepted the packet for relaying but B's receipt is missing, agent A sends a
`TRACE_REQUEST`; three independent neighbours confirm that R accepted the packet and did not pass it on — this forms a Fraud Proof.

**Falsified results.** The random places in search results are calculated verifiably (document 17, section 17.3). A result list in
which a random place does not match the calculation is a ready proof: the contract checks the super-node's signature on it and the
calculation data.

**Forged tables and NodeID hijacking.** An attempt to forge Kademlia DHT records or to impersonate another node is proven by
signatures that do not match the node's key.

## 6.4 Penalties

| Violation | Proof | Penalty |
|---|---|---|
| Downtime | unavailability to neighbours | **none**; the node loses income and after 30 days is removed with its deposit returned |
| Packet dropping | Fraud Proof with a missing receipt | 10% of the deposit |
| Falsified results | results that do not match the verifiable calculation | 25% of the deposit |
| Forged tables, NodeID hijacking | signatures that do not match | 100% of the deposit and permanent exclusion |

**Where the taken coins go.** Half goes to whoever proved the violation: a reward for keeping the network honest. The other half is
removed from circulation for good — as in Bitcoin, where an unclaimed reward is simply lost. No new coins are mined to replace it, so
the final number of coins ends up below 1,000,000,000 by exactly that amount.

```
[Customer agent] --(packet)--> [Super-node R] --X (dropped)--> [Provider agent]
       |                                                              |
       +---------------- (TRACE_REQUEST, waiting for receipt) --------+
                                      |
                              [Fraud Proof]
                                      |
                                      v
                       [ValidatorStaking.sol: slashValidator()]
                                      |
                    +-----------------+-----------------+
                    |                                   |
          (50% to whoever proved it)        (50% removed from circulation)
```

## 6.5 Protection against false reports

So that the contract is not flooded with fake proofs, calling `slashValidator()` requires the reporter to lock a small deposit.

- **The proof is valid:** the reporter gets the deposit back and receives half of the penalty.
- **The proof is false:** the reporter's deposit is removed from circulation.

Honest work pays better than risking the deposit, and a false report costs more than silence.

en.title: 7. Smart Contract Testing and Audit: Foundry, Slither and Fuzzing
en.text:
# 7. Smart Contract Testing and Audit: Foundry, Slither and Fuzzing

Lagrix smart contracts handle real money (USDC) and $LGX coins. A bug in a contract is dangerous: a deployed contract cannot be
"fixed on the fly" without a complex governance procedure. Every contract therefore passes three layers of checks: Foundry tests,
invariant fuzzing and Slither static analysis.

| Contract | What it does | Document |
|---|---|---|
| A2AEscrow.sol | deals, receipts, Time-Lock, fee deduction, the `Receipt` event | 04 |
| FeeDistributor.sol | the fee-return queue for providers and the super-node pool | 09 |
| ReceiptMining.sol | receipts, the right to search for a block, the reward split | 05 |
| LagrixToken.sol | the coin, the supply cap, the six-month rule, the founder's tranches | 05 |
| ValidatorStaking.sol | deposits, removal, penalties, false reports | 06 |
| FeedbackRegistry.sol | likes and dislikes bound to deal receipts | 17 |

## 7.1 Unit and integration tests (Foundry)

Foundry tests are written in Solidity itself and run at the speed of compiled code. Key scenarios:

- `test_A2AEscrow_StateTransitions()` — LOCKED → COMMITTED → COMPLETED transitions and rejection of invalid calls (for example,
  `claimTimeout()` before the dispute window expires).
- `test_EIP712_SignatureReplay()` — a signature cannot be reused with another `taskId` or nonce.
- `test_FeeSplit_95_5()` — on closing, the provider gets exactly 95% and the fee exactly 5%; a refund takes no fee.
- `test_FeeQueue_SkipsInactiveAndOwnProvider()` — the queue skips providers with no deals in 30 days and the provider of the same deal.
- `test_SixMonthRule()` — a coin transfer earlier than 180 days after joining is rejected; after that it passes.
- `test_FounderTranche_12Months()` — a founder's tranche from a block is unavailable before 12 months and available after (`vm.warp()`).
- `test_BlockReward_Split()` — 1% to the founder, then 50/30/20 of the rest, accurate to 1 wei.
- `test_Downtime_NoSlash()` — an unavailable node is not penalised and after 30 days is removed with its deposit returned.
- `test_Slashing_HalfToReporter_HalfRemoved()` — half of a penalty to the reporter, half removed from circulation.

```solidity
// Example: Time-Lock in A2AEscrow.t.sol
function test_CannotClaimTimeoutBeforeDisputePeriod() public {
    vm.prank(customer);
    escrow.lockFunds(taskId, provider, superNode, 100 * 10**6); // lock 100 USDC (6 decimals)

    vm.prank(provider);
    escrow.commitResult(taskId, resultHash);

    // try to collect after 2 minutes, before the 5-minute window expires
    vm.warp(block.timestamp + 2 minutes);

    vm.prank(provider);
    vm.expectRevert(A2AEscrow.DisputePeriodNotExpired.selector);
    escrow.claimTimeout(taskId);
}
```

## 7.2 Fuzzing and invariants

Unit tests check the scenarios the developer thought of. Fuzzing feeds millions of random inputs — edge values, zero addresses, huge
amounts — and checks invariants that must hold for any sequence of calls:

1. **Escrow solvency.** The escrow contract's USDC balance is never below the sum of all locked deals.
2. **Queue solvency.** FeeDistributor's USDC balance is never below the sum of all credited but unclaimed payouts.
3. **Supply cap.** No more than 1,000,000,000 LGX are ever created.
4. **Founder's tranches.** The founder cannot withdraw more than the tranches that are at least 12 months old.
5. **Deposit accounting.** The sum of all super-nodes' deposits equals the total recorded in the staking contract.

```solidity
function invariant_EscrowSolvency() public view {
    assertGe(usdc.balanceOf(address(escrow)), escrow.totalLockedFunds(), "Escrow is insolvent");
}

function invariant_SupplyCap() public view {
    assertLe(token.totalMinted(), 1_000_000_000 * 10**18, "Supply cap exceeded");
}
```

## 7.3 Static analysis (Slither)

Slither translates the code into an intermediate representation and looks for common vulnerabilities:

- **Reentrancy:** protection — the checks → effects → interactions order and OpenZeppelin's `ReentrancyGuard`.
- **Authorization via `tx.origin`:** forbidden; Slither warns about any use of it.
- **Unchecked low-level calls:** token transfers only through `SafeERC20`.
- **Overflows:** built-in checks of Solidity 0.8+ and strict types (`uint96`, `uint40`) for packed fields.

## 7.4 The check pipeline

Every change to the main branch of the open repository goes through the same chain:

```
[ push / pull request ]
       │
       ├──> 1. forge fmt --check               (formatting)
       ├──> 2. slither . --fail-on high|medium  (static analysis)
       ├──> 3. forge test --gas-report          (tests and gas usage)
       └──> 4. forge test --fuzz-runs 10000     (invariant fuzzing)
```

If even one of 10,000 random calls breaks an invariant, the change is not accepted.

en.title: 8. Account Abstraction (ERC-4337): The UserOperation Structure and Bundler Infrastructure
en.text:
# 8. Account Abstraction (ERC-4337): The UserOperation Structure and Bundler Infrastructure

Autonomous AI agents should not manage native blockchain wallets (EOA), having to calculate gas by hand, watch their ETH/MATIC balance and sign raw base transactions. In Lagrix v6.0 we implement an Account Abstraction stack based on the ERC-4337 standard, which turns every AI agent wallet into a programmable smart account (Smart Contract Wallet).

This fully isolates the agent's application logic from blockchain mechanics: the agent operates on a "request-payment" abstraction in USDC, and all the work with network fees is taken over by special aggregator nodes (Bundlers) and the Paymaster contract.

## 8.1 Anatomy of the UserOperation Structure

Instead of standard Ethereum transactions, AI agents form pseudo-transactions — UserOperation (UserOp) objects. The structure packs the agent's intent and is passed over the P2P network of Bundler nodes outside the blockchain's main mempool.

```solidity
struct UserOperation {
    address sender;             // Address of the AI agent's smart account
    uint256 nonce;              // Unique sequential number (Anti-Replay)
    bytes initCode;             // Smart account creation code (if launched for the first time)
    bytes callData;             // Encoded function call (for example, lockFunds in A2AEscrow)
    uint256 callGasLimit;       // Gas limit for executing the application logic
    uint256 verificationGasLimit; // Gas limit for checking signatures and the Paymaster
    uint256 preVerificationGas; // Gas limit to compensate the Bundler's overhead
    uint256 maxFeePerGas;       // Maximum gas price (EIP-1559)
    uint256 maxPriorityFeePerGas;// Tip to the blockchain miner/validator
    bytes paymasterAndData;     // Paymaster contract address + sponsorship signature/conditions
    bytes signature;            // The AI agent's cryptographic signature (secp256k1 / BLS / Passkey)
}
```

Key fields for M2M interaction:

initCode (Lazy Account Deployment): An AI agent is created instantly without transactions on the blockchain. Its smart account is generated off-chain deterministically through CREATE2. The first transaction automatically deploys the account contract thanks to the initCode field.

paymasterAndData: The main integration flag. Contains the address of LagrixPaymaster.sol and parameters indicating that the gas for the transaction is paid not by the agent but by the Paymaster, which deducts the equivalent in USDC.

## 8.2 Bundler Infrastructure: Assembling and Packing Meta-Transactions

A Bundler is a specialized infrastructure node (it can be run by Super-Node operators) that listens to a separate Alt-Mempool for UserOperations.

```
[Client Agent] ---> (UserOp in USDC) ---> [Alt-Mempool (P2P)]
                                                 │
                                                 ▼
                                        [ Bundler Node ]
                                                 │
                             (Packing into a bundle: [UserOp1, UserOp2, ...])
                                                 │
                                                 ▼
                                   [ EntryPoint.sol (On-Chain) ]
                                                 │
                                    ┌────────────┴────────────┐
                                    ▼                         ▼
                          [LagrixPaymaster.sol]       [A2AEscrow.sol]
                         (USDC charged for gas)     (Escrow capture)
```

Step-by-step Bundler algorithm:

Reception and filtering (Validation Phase): The Bundler receives a UserOp through the JSON-RPC method eth_sendUserOperation. It performs an off-chain simulation through the EntryPoint.sol contract, checking:
- The validity of the UserOp.signature.
- That LagrixPaymaster or the agent has a sufficient USDC balance/approval.
- The absence of forbidden opcodes (for example, TIMESTAMP, GASPRICE) that could break execution determinism.

Aggregation (Batching): The Bundler combines 10 to 100 valid UserOps from different AI agents into one standard Ethereum transaction.

Submission to the On-Chain EntryPoint: The Bundler calls the function handleOps(UserOperation[] ops, address beneficiary) on the singleton EntryPoint.sol contract.

Gas compensation: The Bundler pays the native L2 network gas (ETH/Base/Arbitrum) from its own wallet, and the EntryPoint contract instantly compensates its costs from the LagrixPaymaster.sol deposit + accrues a micro-premium (Bundler Fee).

## 8.3 The EntryPoint.sol Contract: The Execution Core

The ERC-4337 standard uses a single EntryPoint contract, proven over the years and deployed at the same addresses in all EVM networks. It acts as a trusted orchestrator.

Lifecycle of a handleOps() call inside EntryPoint:

Verification Loop:
- For each UserOp, the sender account is checked.
- If the account has not been created yet, initCode is executed.
- The validateUserOp() function on the agent's smart account is called to check the ECDSA signature.
- validatePaymasterUserOp() is called on the LagrixPaymaster.sol contract to lock the required amount of USDC to cover gas.

Execution Loop:
- EntryPoint executes the callData of each UserOp (for example, sending a call to A2AEscrow.sol).
- The exact amount of gas actually spent is measured.
- EntryPoint deducts from the Paymaster deposit exactly as much USDC (plus the Bundler premium) as was needed for gas, and returns the unused remainder.

## 8.4 Benefits for the Lagrix Ecosystem

Zero friction (Zero Gas Friction): An AI agent developer only needs to put $10$ USDC on the smart account. The agent will never again need to hold native ETH for transactions.

Session Keys: The agent's smart account makes it possible to limit permissions. A bot can be given a temporary key allowed to spend no more than $1$ USDC per hour and to call exclusively the A2AEscrow.sol contract. If the bot is hacked, the hacker cannot withdraw all the funds from the account.

Atomic Multi-Operations: An agent can do approve(USDC) and lockFunds() in one UserOp, reducing the number of on-chain steps and saving 40% on gas.

en.title: 9. The Deal Fee: Returned to Active Providers, Income for Super-nodes
en.text:
# 9. The Deal Fee: Returned to Active Providers, Income for Super-nodes

The network takes a fee on every deal. This document describes the currency it is taken in, where it goes and how it is distributed.
The $LGX coin plays no part in this mechanism: the fee is money for work, while $LGX is a participant's standing in the network
(ranking, super-node deposit, block rewards, document 05).

## 9.1 Currency: USDC

Agents pay each other for work in USDC (document 04). The fee is taken in the same currency and paid out in it.

| Why USDC | What it gives |
|---|---|
| The fee costs real money from day one | a fake deal with oneself costs 5% of its amount even while $LGX has no price |
| Payouts make sense to people | "10 cents came back", with no conversion at a rate |
| Super-nodes' income does not depend on a rate | in late stages, when mining ends, operators have a stable income |
| No trading of the coin inside the mechanism | the network neither buys nor sells $LGX and does not affect its price |

## 9.2 Rate and moment of collection

The rate is 5% of the deal amount (a parameter the Super-node Council can change within the bounds of the network model, document
18). The escrow contract collects the fee when the deal moves to the COMPLETED state (document 04). If a deal ends in a refund
(REFUNDED), no fee is taken.

## 9.3 Two parts of the fee

Every fee is split into two parts:

```
super_node_share   = coins_mined_so_far / 1,000,000,000
active_queue_share = 1 − super_node_share
```

At the start, while few coins have been mined, almost the whole fee returns to active providers. As coins are mined, the
super-nodes' share grows under any issuance schedule, and by the end of mining (about 30 years) the whole fee goes to them.

## 9.4 The queue of active providers

**Who is in the queue.** A provider who has closed more than three deals as a provider in total and at least one such deal in the last
30 days. The fee is deducted from the provider's payment (document 04), so it is returned to providers — those who keep working.
Customers are rewarded by the network through their share of block rewards (document 05).

**Order.** Providers stand in one shared queue in the order they joined the network. The queue runs in a circle.

**Payout.** The queue part of each new deal's fee is credited in full to the next provider in the queue, and the pointer moves on.
There is no draw: the payout is the fee share of the deal that fell to that turn of the queue.

**Skips.**
- a provider with no deals for more than 30 days is skipped until they close a deal again;
- the provider of the deal the fee came from is skipped too, so the fee never returns to the one it was deducted from.

**Load.** The queue keeps a single pointer, so a payout costs the same for any number of participants. Money is not transferred on
every deal: it is credited to the provider's balance, and they withdraw what has accumulated in one transaction whenever they
choose.

```solidity
// Sketch: crediting a fee share to the next active provider in the queue
function _creditQueue(uint256 amount, address provider) internal {
    for (uint256 i = 0; i < MAX_SKIPS; i++) {
        address next = queue[pointer];
        pointer = (pointer + 1) % queue.length;
        if (next == provider) continue;
        if (dealsAsProvider[next] <= 3 || block.timestamp > lastProviderDealAt[next] + 30 days) continue;
        claimable[next] += amount;               // the provider withdraws it later
        return;
    }
    superNodePool += amount;                      // if no active provider is found, the share goes to super-nodes
}

function claim() external {
    uint256 a = claimable[msg.sender];
    claimable[msg.sender] = 0;
    usdc.safeTransfer(msg.sender, a);
}
```

`MAX_SKIPS` caps the number of skips per deal so that the cost of the operation does not grow.

## 9.5 The super-nodes' share

The super-nodes' share accumulates in a shared pool and is divided among them for each mining period in proportion to their receipts
(document 05, section 5.2). The more deals a super-node has served, the larger its part.

## 9.6 How to talk about it

This is a return of the fee to providers who keep working in the network, and income for those who serve it. The amount of a return is
not known in advance and is not guaranteed by anything: it depends on which deals close in the network and when a provider's turn
in the queue comes.
